references.text: The immediate context where God promises that all flesh will never again be destroyed by floodwaters - a direct parallel to the promise in v. 15.
God establishes His covenant with Noah before the flood, which is the precursor to the covenant confirmed here.
God's promise never again to strike down all living things, forming the basis for the covenant promise in 9:15.
God establishes an everlasting covenant with Abraham and his descendants, demonstrating God's pattern of making enduring covenants with humanity.
God 'remembers' (זָכַר) His covenant, using the same key word as in Gen 9:15, showing God's faithfulness to His covenant promises.
The psalmist reminds us that God remembers His covenant forever, emphasizing God's faithfulness to His covenants, just like with Noah.
Isaiah refers directly to Noah's flood and God's oath that the waters will never again cover the earth - an explicit reference back to Gen 9:15.
The rainbow around the throne in Revelation can be seen as a reminder of God's eternal covenant with Noah.
Isaiah uses God's oath concerning Noah's flood as direct evidence that God's grace toward Israel is now unshakable.
The psalm expresses human fear of the flood that God, in Genesis 9:15, has promised never to send again.
Direct narrative connection: 6:17 is the judgment, and 9:15 is God's promise that this judgment will never be repeated.
Ezekiel uses the same language about God's 'remembering' of the covenant as in Genesis 9:15, linking it to an everlasting covenant.
Hosea expands Noah's covenant with all flesh into a future covenant of peace that also includes the animals.
